==Problem 6==

Sergai skated around an ice rink, gliding along different paths. The gray lines in the figures below show four of the paths labeled P, Q, R, and S. What is the sorted order of the four paths from shortest to longest?

[[Image:2024_AMC_8-Problem_6.png|500px]]

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ P,Q,R,S \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ P,R,S,Q \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ Q,S,P,R \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ R,P,S,Q \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ R,S,P,Q</imath>

==Solution 1==

You can measure the lengths of the paths until you find a couple of guaranteed true inferred statements as such:
<imath>Q</imath> is greater than <imath>S</imath>, 
<imath>P</imath> is greater than <imath>R</imath>, 
and <imath>R</imath> and <imath>P</imath> are the smallest two, therefore the order is <imath>R, P, S, Q.</imath>
Thus we get the answer <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~R, P, S, Q}</imath>.

- U-King



~TabHawaii (minor formatting edits)

==Solution 2 (Intuitive)==

Obviously Path Q is the longest path, followed by Path S. 

So, it is down to Paths P and R.

Notice that curved lines are always longer than the straight ones that meet their endpoints, therefore Path P is longer than Path R.

Thus, the order from shortest to longest is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } \text{R, P, S, Q}}</imath>.

~MrThinker

==Solution 3 (Indepth version of solution 1)==

We can compare paths that look similar, <imath>P</imath> with <imath>R</imath> and <imath>Q</imath> with <imath>S</imath>. 

<imath>R</imath> is shorter than <imath>P</imath> because it replaces curved lines in <imath>P</imath> with straight lines, and straight lines are always the shortest distance between two points. 

The two straight lines in <imath>S</imath> can be seen as paths going diagonally straight across the rink, and the straight lines in <imath>Q</imath> can be seen as initially going diagonally across the rink, before taking a short detour and then finishing its path. Since a straight line between two points is shorter than zig-zagging lines, path <imath>S</imath> is shorter than path <imath>Q</imath>. 

The only difference between path <imath>P</imath> and path <imath>S</imath> is the straight lines, with <imath>P</imath> going up and down while <imath>S</imath> goes diagonally. A right triangle can be drawn from a line from <imath>P</imath> and a line from <imath>S</imath>. We can see that the straight lines in <imath>P</imath> act as the leg of the right triangle while the hypotenuse is the straight lines from <imath>S</imath>. The legs of a right triangle are always less than the hypotenuse, so <imath>P</imath> is shorter than <imath>S</imath>. 

Putting together these inequality statements, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~R, P, S, Q}</imath>.

~Sandcanyon
